title: Disinformation and Misinformation on Twitter during the Novel Coronavirus Outbreak (Huang & Carley, arXiv 2006.04278)
screen_reason: Behavioural platform study of 67.4 million COVID-19 keyword tweets from 12.0 million users (29 Jan - 4 Mar 2020). URLs were matched against Grinberg et al.'s black/red/orange 'fake news' site lists, and Tables 4 and 5 report, per country and overall, the share of English-speaking users in the corpus who posted or retweeted at least one 'fake news' URL (1.60% of source users, 2.50% of retweeters overall; 2.28% and 3.79% in the United States). These are shares of people who shared misinformation at least once, from behavioural data, with explicit denominators.

estimates.country: All countries of English-speaking users in the corpus (table total; top 10 countries listed separately)
estimates.measure_type: % of English-speaking users in the COVID-19 tweet corpus who posted at least one tweet containing a 'fake news' site URL
estimates.value_raw: total 33,514 EN users posting "fake news" URLs out of 2,089,892 EN source users = 1.60% (Table 4, total row)
estimates.denominator: 2,089,892 English-speaking users who posted at least one source tweet in the COVID-19 keyword corpus (67.4M tweets, 12.0M users, of whom 5,448,250 were English-speaking)
estimates.definition: User posted at least one source tweet containing a URL to a site on one of the three 'fake news' lists (black, red, orange) of Grinberg et al.; 20 black, 26 red and 25 orange sites appeared in the data
estimates.misinfo_def: "Following previous work [2] and [14], we define "fake news sites" as ones that "lack the news medias editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information." ... The black list contains a set of websites which published exclusively fabricated stories. The red list is a set of websites spreading falsehoods with a flawed editorial process. Sites labeled as orange represent cases where annotators were less certain that the falsehoods stemmed from a flawed editorial process."
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Third-party domain-reliability lists taken from Grinberg et al. (black = exclusively fabricated; red = falsehoods with a flawed editorial process; orange = annotators less certain), plus a list of 90 trusted news sites. Users' country and language were assigned by a machine-learning user-profiling system (country prediction 92.96% accurate, identity 95.4%, political orientation 87.4%), with geotag majority vote where available (791,830 of 11,951,739 users had geotags).
estimates.moderator_quote: The list include "coronavirus", "coronaravirus", "wuhan virus", "wuhanvirus", "2019nCoV", "NCoV", "NCoV2019". There are 67.4 million tweets and 12.0 million users involved in this time period. ... Because these news lists are mainly compiled by English speakers, we only measured the country distributions among English speaking users to avoid potential language bias.
estimates.notes: CONSTRUCT CALL for an adjudicator: the denominator is PEOPLE, so under the governing denominator rule ('people reached >= 1, behavioural -> REACH') I coded REACH with reach_subtype = sharing. The identical quantity also fits SHARING with sharing_subtype = actor_share ('% of users who shared any'); the two schema branches overlap here and the choice should be made consistently across the corpus. The denominator is not the general population but users already tweeting about COVID-19 in an English-keyword stream, so the base rate is conditional on being in the conversation; denom_scope = population follows the REACH rule regardless. confidence = medium because posting a fake-news URL is counted regardless of whether the tweet endorsed or debunked the link, and because country/language are model-predicted rather than observed. source_quote is the Table 4 total row verbatim (columns: EN users posting fake-news URLs, EN users posting real-news URLs, all EN source users, % posting fake-news URLs); the table caption is quoted separately in page_loc.

missed_or_uncertain:
1) THE MISINFORMATION STORY-LINE MEASURES WERE DELIBERATELY NOT EXTRACTED, and this is the main judgement call. Table 6 gives, per country, the share of English-speaking users who tweeted or retweeted one of five 'misinformation stories' (bio-weapon origin, garlic, sesame oil, bleach, chlorine dioxide) — overall 1.75% of source users and 3.31% of retweeters, and for the U.S. 2.16% and 4.49%. These look like clean shares with denominators, but the authors explicitly disclaim that they measure misinformation spreading: 'we cannot say whether or not the sender of the message is knowingly spreading disinformation, unwittingly spreading misinformation, joking about the story-line (satire), or pointing out that this story-line is not true and so countering disinformation. What we can say is that they are taking part in the discussion around that story-line.' They further note that many bleach tweets 'appeared to be jokes or satirical responses' and that WHO and news agencies were tweeting refutations that the keyword search would capture. The numerator therefore includes debunking and satire, so the measure is topic mention, not misinformation prevalence. If an adjudicator decides such keyword-narrative measures belong in the corpus, the Table 6 values above are ready to use (borderline = true).
2) Country rows beyond the U.S. were not written, to keep the row count proportionate; Table 4 (% of EN source users per country posting fake-news URLs) gives United Kingdom 1.02%, Philippines 0.13%, India 0.40%, Canada 1.77%, Nigeria 1.13%, Australia 1.16%, South Africa 1.29%, Malaysia 0.17%, Kenya 0.43%; Table 5 (retweeters) gives United Kingdom 1.51%, India 0.79%, Philippines 0.12%, Nigeria 2.18%, Canada 2.65%, Malaysia 0.32%, Australia 2.00%, Indonesia 0.16%, South Africa 1.90%. Also stated in text: Hong Kong 2.86% of tweeters and 6.99% of retweeters for misinformation story-lines.
3) No content_share (SHARING) row is extractable. Source tweets with news URLs number 3,085 black + 53,531 red + 61,179 orange + 796,267 real, and retweets 32,305 + 151,286 + 205,409 + 2,739,257, but the paper never states the share of news-URL tweets that were fake-news tweets, and computing 117,795/914,062 = 12.9% would be both a cross-category sum and a denominator I constructed — forbidden by R8. Nor is any share of all 67.4M tweets given.
4) Within-misinformation composition figures, not prevalence: 'About 90% of the tweets containing these "fake news" URLs are initiated by regular users'; '82.45% of people sharing "fake news" URLs are labeled conservative users' (vs 33.28% for real news); '58.74% of the source users sending a URL for a black news site appear to be bots'; the bot percentages in Tables 2 and 3; '73.26% of the English speakers who posted tweets with "fake news" URLs came from United States'. All are shares of the misinformation set, not of a population or content universe.
5) Cross-country retweet shares (26.69% of real-news retweeters are in a different country from the source; 36.38% of inter-country retweets originate in the U.S.; 56.98% for bio-weapon, 71.25% bleach, 89.6% chlorine dioxide, 50.43% of sesame retweets from Switzerland) describe geography of flow, not prevalence.
6) CONCENTRATION: nothing usable. The paper reports influence distributions (25.98% of the top 10,000 tweets by news agencies, 90% of the top 100 by regular users) but never a top-X%-of-users to Y%-of-misinformation pairing, so R1 cannot be satisfied. The Grinberg and Gupta concentration findings mentioned in the introduction are cited from elsewhere.
7) Bot prevalence (28.6% of 5,448,250 English-speaking users exhibit bot-like characteristics) is not a misinformation share.

rob.design: Large-scale observational platform study. Twitter real-time filter stream on seven COVID-19 keywords ('coronavirus', 'coronaravirus', 'wuhan virus', 'wuhanvirus', '2019nCoV', 'NCoV', 'NCoV2019'), 29 Jan - 4 Mar 2020: 67,408,573 tweets from 12,047,990 users; timelines (most recent 200 tweets) and follow ties collected for 11,951,739 of them. Misinformation operationalised two ways: (a) URLs matched to Grinberg et al.'s black (20), red (26) and orange (25) 'fake news' site lists against 90 trusted news sites; (b) keyword retrieval of five manually identified disinformation story-lines. User attributes are MODEL-PREDICTED, not observed: home country (92.96% accuracy; geotag majority vote for the 791,830 users with geotags), social identity in seven classes (95.4%), political orientation (87.4%), bot-likeness via bot-hunter at a 60% cutoff (precision .957, recall .704). Identity and orientation classifiers applied only to English-majority users; country shares computed only for English speakers to limit language bias. Acknowledged limits: English-keyword bias in both the stream and the domain lists, keyword selection under-samples story-line discussion, and story-line tweets may endorse, joke about, or debunk the claim. No human coding of tweet content and no interrater reliability (none applicable to a list-based design).
rob.item6_quote: Following previous work [2] and [14], we define "fake news sites" as ones that "lack the news medias editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information." We adopt three lists of "fake news" sites as proposed in [14]: black sites, orange sites, red sites.
rob.item10_quote: To partially control for this bias, we normalize the number of users sharing "fake news" URLs by the total number of users in each country. The last column of Table 4 shows the normalized results. The probability for each U.S. user posting a "fake news" URL is 2.28%, while the probabilities for Philippines and Malaysia are 0.13% and 0.17%.
